scenario: Today’s personalization track looks past a single scoring model to the system around it. Long histories are compressed into reusable online features, the cascade from retrieval to re-ranking can be orchestrated per user without making a live request wait on a language model, and the ranker itself is beginning to be changed, trained, and evaluated by human-on-the-loop agents. Policy experiments should spend samples on the actions where two policies actually diverge, rather than on the overlap both would have chosen. Item side information has to resist inversion while keeping relative relations, long-tail items have to be retrieved before anyone decides whether to call a language model, and even interaction intensity can be ranked over the full candidate set on a dynamic graph. The shared question is this: once personalization leaves the place where it was validated, serving budgets, experiment design, and privacy constraints will rewrite it.

papers.title: X-split Argus: Learning Reusable History Tokens for Efficient CTR Prediction
papers.authors: Alexander Ploshkin, Nikita Stepanov, Alexey Pismenny, Viacheslav Ovchinnikov, Nikolay Savushkin
papers.summary: Industrial ad click-through prediction has to capture both long-term preferences and recent intent, but recomputing a user’s full behavioral history for every candidate is hard to afford under compute and latency limits. One ad-ranking framework trains a history compressor and an online ranker together. Past interactions are compressed offline into a reusable set of history tokens, and the online ranker scores ads by attending to those tokens and recent events, so long histories are not rescanned for every candidate. Offline, normalized entropy falls 0.81% relative to the production model. After deployment in a large real-time bidding system, a seven-day A/B test raises a metric of advertisers’ conversion value by 4.65% and clicks by 2.96%, while serving the same traffic uses about 15% more online GPUs of the same type. ==Long histories have to be compressed into reusable offline features before ranking can be made richer inside a budget.==
papers.abstract: Accurate click-through rate (CTR) prediction depends on user representations that capture both persistent preferences and recent intent, yet processing extensive behavioral histories for every ranking request is costly under production compute and latency constraints. We present X-split ARGUS, a framework for ad ranking whose history compressor and online ranker are trained end to end. The compressor encodes past interactions into a compact set of tokens that are computed offline and reused across candidates, while the online ranker scores ads through cross-attention to these tokens and representations of recent events. Training combines an autoregressive loss for click feedback with distillation of candidate-specific click logits from a larger teacher that scores each candidate using the uncompressed history. The number of compressed history tokens and the length of recent history can be adjusted to fit serving compute and latency budgets. Offline evaluation shows a 0.81% relative red
papers.score_note: 工业广告 CTR：离线 NE -0.81%，线上 A/B 转化价值 +4.65%、点击 +2.96%；历史 token 离线压缩+在线 cross-attention。未见开源，实用性记 4 而非 5。

papers.title: MARS Technical Report
papers.authors: Tong Liu, Chaoqun Hou, Longxiang Xiong, Junhong Lou, Jiaqi Zheng, Qixin Li, Zixin Zhao, Yong Duan, Xiannian Hu, Fengze Jiang, Yu Zhu, Cheng Guo, Xinyuan Qi, Zi Zhuang, Ping Liu, Lv Shao, Zongwei Wang
papers.summary: Industrial recommenders usually run as a cascade of retrieval, pre-ranking, ranking, and re-ranking. Decisions about which channels to open, how to set quotas, which models to use, and how to fuse scores are still often tuned by engineers once per scenario and shared by every user. A near-line agent extends personalization from stage-wise scoring to orchestration of the whole pipeline: it writes a seven-dimensional configuration for each user, validates it, and caches it, so the online cascade reads the result asynchronously and never waits for a live language-model call. In two-week A/B tests across five Taobao marketing scenarios with more than ten million daily active users, every scenario’s key metrics have a positive point estimate. The largest relative gains are 5.22% in the share of exposed users who purchase and 7.34% in gross merchandise value, and mean online serving-path latency is also 12 milliseconds lower than the production baseline. ==How the cascade runs can be personalized too, without making online requests wait on a language model.==
papers.abstract: Modern industrial recommender systems use multi-stage cascades--retrieval, pre-ranking, ranking, and re-ranking--to narrow millions of candidates to a personalized list. While each stage deploys sophisticated models, pipeline-level decisions on channel activation, quotas, model selection, and score fusion remain engineer-tuned and user-agnostic within each scenario. This report presents MARS (Multi-stage Agentic Recommendation System), extending personalization from individual-stage predictions to full pipeline orchestration. A near-line agent built on fine-tuned Qwen3-0.6B generates per-user configurations--a seven-dimensional action covering pipeline mode, retrieval quotas, model selection, fusion weights, and reranker settings--from a constrained action space. Configurations are validated, cached, and consumed asynchronously; the cascade never waits for LLM inference. Schema checks, fallbacks, and a kill switch ensure serving safety. papers.title: MLE Agents: Autonomous ML Engineering in Large-scale Recommendation Systems
papers.authors: Matthew Li, Albert Liang, Dilip Raj
papers.summary: Improving a large-scale search ranker or recommender usually means an engineer forms a hypothesis, edits code, trains a model, and evaluates it, a slow loop that also tends to stay inside familiar directions. Human-on-the-loop machine-learning-engineer agents can propose a change, write it as code, launch training, read the offline evaluation, and decide whether to keep it on an industrial search ranker, while people still control the objective, the search direction, and final-model review. In one campaign the system finished 1097 candidate experiments and accepted 29.6% of them, compared with 15.6% in an earlier campaign that used a different objective and search constraint. The best model raised search volume by 0.23% in a large-scale A/B test, and some of the accepted changes were architectural ideas the team had not previously tried on this stack. ==In industrial model iteration, how the loop is designed is often as important as the base model itself.==
papers.abstract: The typical workflow for improving large-scale ranking and recommendation models is slow and tedious: an engineer forms a hypothesis, implements it as a code change, trains a model, and evaluates it both offline and online, often relying on their own intuition and experience along the way. Autonomous LLM agents promise to speed this up by running the loop on their own, but it is still unclear whether they can do this in industry-scale systems rather than on benchmarks or small proxy tasks. We build human-on-the-loop machine learning engineer (MLE) agents that propose, implement, train, and evaluate model changes on large-scale search rankers. Engineers retain control over objective design, search direction, and final-model review. We identify three obstacles that make this industry setting challenging: feedback takes hours per experiment, offline metrics do not always predict online impact, and improvements saturate after the early wins. papers.title: Variance-Optimal Counterfactual Policy Design for Sample-Efficient Online A/B Testing
papers.summary: A new recommendation or ranking policy is usually compared with production in an A/B test, but when the two policies often choose the same action, those overlapping observations add noise while saying little about the difference, so the test needs a lot of traffic. Most variance-reduction methods improve the estimator only after the collection plan is fixed, or they optimize a single traffic split between the two policies, and therefore cannot send samples to the actions on which the policies disagree. This design jointly optimizes how actions are sampled and how the observations are used to estimate the treatment effect, and it uses historical logs to fit a control variate. In simulated policy A/B tests, a model-based control-variate design reaches the mean squared error of a balanced test with 39% to 51% of the evaluation traffic. With ten thousand evaluation interactions, it raises statistical power to 1.5 to 2.1 times that of balanced A/B testing. ==A policy test should spend its samples where the two policies actually diverge.==
papers.abstract: Online A/B testing is the standard approach for evaluating changes to user-facing systems, such as a new recommendation or ranking policy, before deployment. While the difference-in-means estimator of a standard A/B test is unbiased, it often suffers from high variance. When the treatment and production policies choose the same actions with similar probabilities, the resulting observations can add noise while providing little information about the difference between the policies. Consequently, A/B tests can require large amounts of traffic and long durations to detect small treatment effects. Existing variance-reduction methods mainly improve the estimator after the data-collection scheme has been fixed, and recent overlap-aware designs only optimize a single traffic split between the two policies; thereby, they cannot direct traffic to the actions on which the policies disagree. papers.title: PGPO: Prototype-Guided Progressive Obfuscation for Privacy-Preserving LLM-Enhanced Recommendation
papers.authors: Shengxiang Lin, Jiajie Su, Pengyang Zhou, Xiang Chen, Xiaolin Zheng, Feng Tian, Chaochao Chen
papers.summary: LLM-enhanced recommenders encode item side information into semantic embeddings, but those embeddings can leak sensitive attributes through inversion attacks. Existing input-side defenses rely on trusted collection or local token perturbation, and they often scramble the relative topology among items that recommendation needs. The aim here is relational fidelity: the semantics should shift enough to resist inversion, while relative item relations are preserved. The method learns topology-aware obfuscation anchors for high-influence prototype words, propagates them over a static semantic graph, and optimizes them with rewards for individual dissimilarity, structural consistency, and semantic constraint. On two benchmarks, obfuscation methods cut inversion-attack success by more than 50% relative to raw descriptions; for traditional collaborative filtering models, the drop from the upper bound that uses the original text is typically below 2%, and downstream utility stays stronger than token-level perturbation. ==Privacy need not be bought by tearing up relations among items.==
papers.abstract: LLM-enhanced recommender systems encode item side information into semantic embeddings, but these embeddings may leak sensitive textual attributes through inversion attacks. Existing input-side defenses rely on trusted collection or local token perturbation, often disrupting the inter-item semantic topology needed for recommendation. To address it, we introduce relational fidelity as the key objective, requiring semantic shift for privacy while preserving relative item relations for utility. Based on this principle, we propose prototype-guided progressive obfuscation (PGPO), which learns topology-aware obfuscation anchors for high-influence prototype words and propagates them through a static semantic graph. PGPO is optimized with GRPO using individual dissimilarity, structural consistency, and semantic constraint rewards. Experiments on two benchmarks show strong inversion defense with near-upper-bound recommendation performance. The code is available at https://github.com/Shengxiang-

papers.title: AgentTailor: Dual-Gate LLM-Assisted Re-ranking for Personalized Long-Tail Recommendation
papers.authors: Jinpeng Chen, Zhenye Yang, Huan Li, Kaimin Wei, Senzhang Wang, Hongbo Gao
papers.summary: Recommender systems easily let head items dominate exposure while many long-tail items barely appear. Existing long-tail methods often rely on global reweighting or on opaque rankers, which makes it hard to raise tail exposure in a personalized way without hurting overall utility. A modular LLM-assisted framework splits the job into two stages. Semantic recall first retrieves a semantically aligned candidate pool, so relevant long-tail items can reach later ranking, and a conditional tail-specialist branch then re-ranks with evidence when it is needed. That branch uses a dual gate to regulate tail pressure. An activation gate decides whether to invoke the language model for evidence-based assessment, and a placement gate decides whether the extracted evidence is allowed into the final ranking. ==Long-tail items have to be retrieved first; only then is it worth deciding whether to call a language model for them.==
papers.abstract: Recommender systems are central to modern digital platforms but remain vulnerable to popularity bias, where head items dominate exposure while many long-tail items are underrepresented. Existing long-tail methods often rely on global reweighting or opaque ranking models, making it difficult to personalize tail exposure without degrading recommendation utility. To address this challenge, we propose AgentTailor, a modular LLM-assisted framework for personalized long-tail recommendation. AgentTailor decomposes recommendation into two complementary stages. First, a semantic recall module retrieves a semantically aligned candidate pool, determining whether relevant long-tail items are accessible to later ranking. papers.title: DyNA-Mixer: Decoupling Time and Topology for Scalable Dynamic Node Affinity Prediction
papers.authors: Yuanxing Zheng, Liping Wang, Xuemin Lin
papers.summary: Continuous-time dynamic graphs keep the order, timing, and strength of interactions that matter for recommenders, trade networks, and transaction platforms, but research has long focused on dynamic link prediction, which only forecasts whether a future link will occur. Many applications also need the intensity of that interaction and a ranking over all candidates. Dynamic node affinity prediction generalizes the task to continuous targets and full-candidate ranking, which requires modeling multi-scale temporal change and graph-wide collaboration without running an expensive forecast on every node pair. One method decouples temporal forecasting from collaborative structure: a multi-scale temporal predictor tracks pair-specific affinity over time, a virtual collaborative graph aggregates related interactions at query time, and a sparse strategy runs the costly forecast only on pairs with recent non-zero affinity. It reports state-of-the-art NDCG@10 on all four temporal graph benchmarks, including a 17.8% relative test-set gain over the strongest baseline on tgbn-token, the largest dataset. ==Intensity prediction can rank the full candidate set without charging every node pair the same compute.==
papers.abstract: Continuous-time dynamic graphs preserve the ordering, timing, and evolving strength of interactions that static snapshots discard, making dynamic graph mining essential for evolving systems such as recommender systems, trade networks, and transaction platforms. Research in this area has centered on dynamic link prediction, which forecasts only whether a future interaction will occur, whereas many applications also need its intensity. The dynamic node affinity prediction (DNAP) problem generalizes this task to continuous targets and full-candidate ranking, making it more broadly applicable but substantially harder. This raises two coupled difficulties: ranking requires a predictor expressive enough to capture both multi-scale temporal evolution and graph-wide collaborative patterns, yet running such a predictor over every source--destination pair is computationally prohibitive.
